title: Atrioventricular canal defects: anatomy, Rastelli classification, two-patch repair and LVOT obstruction
subject: ss-ctvs

Congenital Heart Surgery Nomenclature and Database Project: AVSD

steps.say: Atrioventricular septal defects result from failed embryological development of the endocardial cushions. Failure of the superior and inferior endocardial cushions to fuse creates a common atrioventricular valve junction and an unwound, scoop-shaped ventricular septum. This abnormal geometry produces a characteristically elongated left ventricular outflow tract.
steps.tx: An **AV canal defect** arises from deficient embryonic fusion of the superior and inferior **endocardial cushions**. The resulting anatomical defect features a scoop-shaped deficiency of the inlet ventricular septum, a common atrioventricular junction, and an anteriorly displaced, **elongated LVOT** predisposing to subaortic stenosis.

steps.say: Partial atrioventricular canal defect consists of an ostium primum atrial septal defect and two separate atrioventricular valve orifices. The anterior leaflet of the left atrioventricular valve contains a prominent cleft pointing directly toward the ventricular septum. The underlying inlet ventricular septum remains intact without shunting.
steps.tx: In **partial AV canal**, the clinical anatomy consists of an **ostium primum ASD**, two distinct atrioventricular valve orifices partitioned by a central fibrous bridge, and a characteristic **mitral cleft** within the anterior left atrioventricular valve leaflet oriented directly toward the mid-interventricular septum.

left.title: Partial AV Canal
points: Divided valve orifices with left AV valve cleft
Intact inlet ventricular septum without shunt

right.title: Complete AV Canal
points: Confluent primum ASD and large inlet VSD
Single common atrioventricular valve with 5 leaflets

steps.say: Complete atrioventricular canal defect features a confluent ostium primum ASD and a large inlet ventricular septal defect. A single common atrioventricular valve with five leaflets spans both ventricular chambers. Massive left-to-right shunting causes severe pulmonary overcirculation and rapid cardiac enlargement.
steps.tx: A **complete AV canal** features an unrestrictive **inlet VSD**, a confluent ostium primum defect, and a single **common AV valve** with 5 primary leaflets (anterior and posterior bridging leaflets, two lateral mural leaflets, and a right lateral leaflet) straddling the interventricular crest.

rows: Massive biventricular volume and pressure overload
Severe regurgitation, pulmonary overcirculation, and failure to thrive

steps.say: Complete canal defects occur in up to forty percent of children with Down syndrome. Trisomy 21 confers an exceptional predisposition to accelerated pulmonary vascular obstructive disease. Because irreversible vascular changes develop very early, surgical repair is strongly indicated by three to six months of age.
steps.tx: Complete canal defects occur in 40 percent of infants with **trisomy 21** or **Down syndrome**. These patients exhibit heightened pulmonary vascular reactivity and develop accelerated **pulmonary vascular disease**; therefore, definitive surgical correction is routinely performed by 3 to 6 months of age to prevent irreversible Eisenmenger syndrome.

nodes.label: Infant with trisomy 21 and complete AV canal defect
Medical management with diuretics and high-calorie feeding
Echocardiography monitors pulmonary artery pressures and valve competence
Perform definitive surgical repair between 3 and 6 months of age

steps.say: The Rastelli classification categorizes complete canal defects based on chordal anatomy of the anterior bridging leaflet. Type A features leaflets tethered directly to the crest of the septum. Type B has chordae attached to an abnormal right ventricular papillary muscle. Type C has a completely free-floating anterior bridging leaflet.
steps.tx: The **Rastelli classification** categorizes complete defects according to anterior **bridging leaflet** chordal morphology. **Type A** has chordae attached directly to the septal crest. Type B features chordae anchoring to an anomalous RV papillary muscle, while **Type C** exhibits a large, free-floating unattached leaflet commonly associated with tetralogy of Fallot.

rows: Leaflet divided; tethered to crest of ventricular septum
Chordae attach to anomalous right ventricular papillary muscle
Challenging division; risk of RV outflow compromise
Large undivided leaflet floating free across septum
Requires extensive central leaflet division and patch suspension

steps.say: Surgical repair can be performed using a classic two-patch technique or a modified single-patch technique. The two-patch technique uses Dacron or polytetrafluoroethylene for the inlet VSD and autologous pericardium for the primum ASD. Dividing and suspending the bridging leaflets onto the patch ensures competence.
steps.tx: Definitive repair uses a **two-patch technique** (Dacron or PTFE for the inlet VSD and treated autologous pericardium for the primum ASD) or a **modified single-patch** technique. Both approaches require precise **leaflet suspension** onto the patch at the level of the ventricular crest to partition the common valve into competent right and left orifices.

left.title: Two-Patch Technique
points: Separate rigid prosthetic patch for inlet VSD
Autologous pericardial patch for primum ASD
Optimal geometry for large inlet ventricular defects

right.title: Modified Single-Patch (Australian)
points: Directly sandwiches leaflets to crest of ventricular septum
Pericardial patch closes only the primum ASD component
Significantly shorter cross-clamp and bypass duration

steps.say: Closing the cleft in the left atrioventricular valve restores valve competence. The cleft is approximated with interrupted non-absorbable sutures, taking care not to produce mitral stenosis. Suture placement along the posterior ventricular crest must avoid the specialized conduction system to prevent complete heart block.
steps.tx: Meticulous **cleft closure** of the left atrioventricular valve with interrupted sutures achieves **left AV valve competence** without narrowing the orifice. Concurrently, careful suture placement away from the posteroinferior crest ensures **conduction tissue avoidance**, protecting the displaced atrioventricular node and bundle of His.

nodes.label: Suspend bridging leaflets at crest of ventricular septal patch
Reapproximate left-sided cleft edges with interrupted polypropylene
Test left AV valve competence by saline distension of ventricle
Close primum ASD patch avoiding posteroinferior nodal triangle

steps.say: Subaortic stenosis is a recognized late complication following surgical repair. The anatomical deficiency of the inlet septum unwinds the left ventricular outflow tract, producing a classic goose-neck deformity on angiography. Narrowing develops in five to ten percent of patients, occasionally requiring late reoperation.
steps.tx: An unwound, narrowed left ventricular outflow tract manifests as a characteristic **goose-neck deformity** on angiographic imaging. This anatomical distortion causes secondary **LVOT narrowing** and late **subaortic stenosis** in 5 to 10 percent of postoperative patients, which may require late surgical resection or reoperation.
